title: How do you map a domain name to a load balancer (Route 53 alias record vs CNAME), and why prefer an alias record for an AWS resource?
shortTitle: Mapping a Domain to a Load Balancer: Alias Record vs CNAME
keyPoints: An ALB gives a DNS name, not a fixed IP, so you must map your domain to that name rather than to an IP address.
A CNAME maps a name to another name but cannot sit at the zone apex (the naked domain) and adds an extra DNS resolution step.
A Route 53 alias record maps a name directly to the AWS resource's IPs, is allowed at the zone apex, and tracks changing IPs automatically.
Alias queries to AWS resources are free, while CNAME queries may incur standard DNS charges.
Alias records only work within Route 53 and only to supported AWS targets (ALB, NLB, CloudFront, S3, API Gateway).
If DNS is hosted outside Route 53, you are forced to use a CNAME on a subdomain and cannot alias the apex.

s1_definition.oneliner: A CNAME points a name to another name with an extra lookup and cannot sit at the root domain, while a Route 53 alias points straight to the AWS resource's IPs at the root domain, for free, and tracks its changing addresses automatically.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **CNAME record** – a DNS record that maps one domain name to another; the resolver does a second lookup to get the actual IP, and DNS rules forbid a CNAME at the zone apex.
- **Route 53 alias record** – an AWS-specific extension that maps a name directly to an AWS resource's IP addresses inside Route 53; allowed at the zone apex, free for AWS resource queries, and tracks changing IPs automatically.
- **Zone apex** – the naked domain like `bank.example.com` with no subdomain prefix (no `www`).
- **Supported alias targets** – ALB, NLB, CloudFront, S3 website endpoint, API Gateway, and another Route 53 record in the same zone.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine `bank.example.com` is the public name of National Bank of India. A CNAME is like telling a customer "to reach the internet banking desk, first call the central directory, and they will give you another number to call, and only then will you reach a counter." It is an extra hop. An alias record is like the directory knowing the actual counter numbers directly, so when Rajesh asks for internet banking it gives him the real numbers in one step, and if the bank adds or removes counters, the directory is updated automatically.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
          CNAME vs Alias Record Resolution

  CNAME (two steps, subdomain only):
  ┌─────────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐
  │ Client      │───→│ DNS Resolver      │───→│ bank.example │
  │ resolves    │    │                   │    │ .com NS      │
  │ www.bank.   │    │ Step 1: get CNAME │    │              │
  │ example.com │    │ www → alb-123.elb │    │ Returns:     │
  │             │    │                   │    │ CNAME record │
  │             │    │ Step 2: resolve   │    └──────────────┘
  │             │    │ alb-123.elb.com   │
  │             │    │ → 52.10.1.100     │    Extra lookup!
  │             │    │                   │    Cannot be at
  └─────────────┘    └──────────────────┘    zone apex!


  Alias (one step, apex allowed):
  ┌─────────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐
  │ Client      │───→│ Route 53          │───→│ Route 53     │
  │ resolves    │    │                   │    │ knows ALB    │
  │ bank.       │    │ Alias → ALB       │    │ resource     │
  │ example.com │    │ Resolves INTERNALLY│    │              │
  │ (apex!)     │    │ to current IPs    │    │ Returns:     │
  │             │    │                   │    │ A record(s)  │
  │             │    │ Returns A records │    │ directly     │
  └─────────────┘    └──────────────────┘    └──────────────┘
                     One step! Free! Auto-tracks IP changes!
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To point a domain at an AWS load balancer I create a DNS record in Route 53, and I have two options: a CNAME record or a Route 53 alias record. A load balancer does not give me a fixed IP; it gives me a long DNS name whose underlying IPs change as AWS scales it, so I must map my friendly domain to the resource, never to a hardcoded IP.

A CNAME record maps a name to another name. It works for a subdomain like `www`, but it has two drawbacks. First, DNS rules forbid a CNAME at the zone apex, so I cannot map the naked `bank.example.com` with a CNAME. Second, the client has to do a second DNS lookup to turn the target name into an IP, which adds a resolution step.

A Route 53 alias record is an AWS-specific extension that maps the name straight to the AWS resource. Route 53 resolves it internally to the load balancer's current IP addresses and hands the client A records directly in one step. I prefer it for three reasons: it is allowed at the zone apex so I can use the clean naked domain, alias queries to AWS resources are free, and it automatically tracks the load balancer's changing IPs.

At National Bank of India I wanted customers to reach internet banking at the clean `bank.example.com` with no `www`, behind an Application Load Balancer. A CNAME cannot sit at that apex, so I used a Route 53 alias A record. That gave customers the naked domain, saved the extra lookup, and meant that when AWS changed the load balancer's IPs our DNS resolved correctly with no manual change.

Remember one sentence: use a Route 53 alias record instead of a CNAME to map a domain to an AWS load balancer, because it works at the zone apex, resolves in one step, is free, and tracks changing IPs automatically.
